Enough
ĕ-nŭf'
adj. and n. (sufficient; as much as is required — and in Scripture, the confession the covetous heart never makes)
From Anglo-Saxon genoh, sufficient, from a root meaning to attain or to reach. The word originally described arriving at a required measure, not an abundance beyond it.

Biblical Definition

Enough in Scripture is a matter of the heart rather than the ledger. Esau, reconciled to his brother and offered a present, says the words the covetous cannot say: “I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself” (Gen 33:9). At the building of the tabernacle the people bring so much that the workmen have to be restrained — “the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much” (Exo 36:7) — the only recorded instance in Scripture of a building fund being closed for excess of giving. Proverbs names the opposite condition with a memorable image: “The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough” (Pro 30:15). And the prodigal's turning point is an act of arithmetic about enough: “How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!” (Luk 15:17). He comes to himself by remembering a house where there was enough, and the road home begins there.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines enough as that which satisfies desire, or gives content; sufficient; equal to the powers or abilities — and notes it as both adjective and noun.

expand to see more

ENOUGH, a. That satisfies desire, or gives content; that may answer the purpose; sufficient.

ENOUGH, n. A sufficiency; a quantity of a thing which satisfies desire, or is adequate to the wants.

I have enough, my brother. Gen. xxxiii.

ENOUGH, adv. Sufficiently; in a quantity or degree that satisfies.

Note. From the Saxon genoh, sufficient; the primary sense is to reach or attain.

Key Scripture

Gen 33:9 — "And Esau said, I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself."

Exo 36:7 — "For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much."

Pro 30:15 — "The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough:"

Luk 15:17 — "And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!"

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel makes more the standing evidence of God's favour, so that a Christian is taught never to say enough and to read contentment as small faith.

expand to see more

Where increase is preached as the reliable sign of blessing, the horseleach of Pro 30:15 is installed in the pulpit. The seed-faith appeal works precisely by ensuring that no giver ever arrives at enough: the offering is always a deposit against a larger return, so the appetite is fed rather than mortified. Scripture's pattern in Exo 36:7 is the exact reverse — a collection stopped by proclamation because the people had brought too much. It is worth asking when a modern ministry last restrained its own giving.

Against this stands the plain apostolic standard: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8), and “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:6). Enough is not a low ambition; it is the floor from which generosity becomes possible, since a man who has enough has something to give. And Luk 15:17 shows the doctrine at its most pastoral. The prodigal does not repent because he calculates a better return; he repents because he remembers a father's house where the hired servants had bread enough and to spare. The memory of sufficiency in the father's house is what turns him around, and it is the same memory that turns any sinner around.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon genoh, sufficient; rendering Hebrew rab (H7227), much, enough, and day (H1767), sufficiency, and Greek arkeo (G714), to suffice, and perisseuo (G4052), to abound.

expand to see more

Anglo-Saxon genoh — sufficient; from a root meaning to reach or attain a required measure.

Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, many, enough; Esau's “I have enough” (Gen 33:9) is yesh li rab, “I have much”.

Hebrew day (H1767) — sufficiency; the root behind El Shaddai in one traditional derivation, God the all-sufficient.

Hebrew hon in Pro 30:15 — the four things that “say not, It is enough”: the grave, the barren womb, the earth, and the fire.

Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, have over and above; “bread enough and to spare” (Luk 15:17).

Usage

"“I have enough, my brother” — the sentence a covetous heart cannot form."

"“Sufficient for all the work… and too much” — the one collection Scripture records being closed."

"“Say not, It is enough” — the grave, the womb, the earth, and the fire; and the covetous man among them."
